title: Digital Logic Basics
summary: The tiny switches under every CPU. Learn logic gates, how they combine into adders and memory, and what a clock does.

blocks.markdown:
**Digital logic** is the layer of tiny on/off switches that every computer is built from.

- A **bit** is one binary digit: 0 or 1, off or on.
- A **logic gate** takes bits in and produces a bit out, following a fixed rule.
- Gates combine into **circuits** that add numbers, store bits, and move data.
- Millions of these switches, working together, are what make a CPU compute.

blocks.subTitle: The two big categories
blocks.markdown:
Every circuit you'll meet falls into one of two kinds.

| Kind | Output depends on |
|---|---|
| Combinational | Current inputs only |
| Sequential | Current inputs + stored state |

Combinational logic computes; sequential logic remembers.

blocks.subTitle: AND, OR, NOT
blocks.markdown:
A **logic gate** is a tiny circuit that turns one or two input bits into one output bit.

- **AND** — output 1 only if **both** inputs are 1.
- **OR** — output 1 if **at least one** input is 1.
- **NOT** — flips a single input: 0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0.

These three are the base; every other gate can be built from them.

blocks.subTitle: NAND, NOR, XOR
blocks.markdown:
Three more gates, each an AND/OR/NOT variant.

- **NAND** — AND, then flipped: 0 only when both inputs are 1.
- **NOR** — OR, then flipped: 1 only when both inputs are 0.
- **XOR** — 1 only when the inputs **differ** (exclusive or).

NAND is special: every other gate can be built using only NAND gates.

blocks.subTitle: Reading a truth table
blocks.markdown:
A **truth table** lists every input combination and the gate's output for each.

| A | B | A AND B |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |

This is how a gate's behavior is defined exactly, with no ambiguity.

The split that organizes all digital logic.

- **Combinational** — pure function of current inputs; no memory (adders, decoders).
- **Sequential** — output depends on inputs **and** stored state from before (registers, counters).

Sequential logic needs a way to store a bit — that's what latches and flip-flops do next. See [cpu-datapath](cpu-datapath).

blocks.subTitle: Half adder
blocks.markdown:
A **half adder** adds two single bits and produces a sum and a carry.

- **Sum** = A XOR B.
- **Carry** = A AND B (1 only when both bits are 1, like carrying in decimal addition).
- It's called "half" because it can't accept a carry-in from a previous column.

blocks.subTitle: Full adder
blocks.markdown:
A **full adder** adds two bits **plus a carry-in**, so adders can be chained to add multi-bit numbers.

Chain several full adders together and you can add whole binary numbers, one bit-column at a time.

blocks.subTitle: Multiplexer
blocks.markdown:
A **multiplexer (mux)** picks one of several input signals to pass through, based on a **select** input.

- A 2-to-1 mux has two data inputs, one select bit, and one output.
- Select = 0 → pass input A. Select = 1 → pass input B.
- Used everywhere a circuit must choose between data sources, like an ALU picking an operation's result.

blocks.subTitle: Decoder
blocks.markdown:
A **decoder** takes a binary code in and activates exactly one of many outputs.

- A 2-bit input can select 1 of 4 outputs (2-to-4 decoder).
- Used to turn an address into "which memory chip" or "which register" to activate.

A mux **selects among** signals; a decoder **activates one** output — opposite jobs.

blocks.subTitle: Latches and flip-flops
blocks.markdown:
Both **store a single bit**, but they update at different times.

- **Latch** — transparent: output follows input any time it's enabled.
- **Flip-flop** — updates only on a **clock edge** (the instant the clock ticks from 0 to 1, or 1 to 0).

CPUs use flip-flops almost everywhere, since edge timing keeps circuits predictable.

blocks.subTitle: Registers
blocks.markdown:
A **register** is a group of flip-flops wired together to store one multi-bit value.

- An 8-bit register holds one byte, updated in one clock tick.
- CPUs use registers to hold values being worked on right now — the fastest storage a CPU has.
- Building block for the CPU's datapath. See [cpu-datapath](cpu-datapath).

The **clock** is a signal that ticks between 0 and 1 at a steady rate, keeping every flip-flop in sync.

- On each tick, flip-flops capture new values all at once.
- **Clock speed** (e.g. 3 GHz) is how many ticks happen per second.
- Without a shared clock, sequential circuits would update at random times and produce garbage.

A CPU is gates and flip-flops stacked in layers.

- Gates combine into an **ALU** (does math and logic on numbers).
- Flip-flops combine into **registers** (hold values between steps).
- The **clock** steps everything forward together, instruction by instruction.

Nothing magic happens above this — it's all switches, just billions of them.

Common mix-ups:

- **"Latch and flip-flop are the same."** No — a latch is level-sensitive, a flip-flop is edge-triggered.
- **"A mux and a decoder do the same thing."** No — a mux selects one signal to output; a decoder activates one output line.
- **"More gates always means slower."** Not directly — depth of the longest gate path matters more than gate count.

blocks.subTitle: Combinational vs sequential
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between combinational and sequential logic?**

Combinational logic's output depends only on the current inputs — no memory (an adder, a mux). Sequential logic's output depends on current inputs **plus** stored state from before (a register, a counter), so it needs a clock to know when to update.

blocks.subTitle: What a flip-flop does
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What does a flip-flop do, in plain terms?**

It stores one bit, and only changes that bit on a clock edge — the exact instant the clock signal flips. Between edges, it holds its value steady, which is what lets a CPU keep a stable value while the rest of the circuit is still computing the next one.

blocks.subTitle: Why NAND is universal
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why is NAND called a "universal" gate?**

Because AND, OR, and NOT can each be built using only NAND gates wired together — so a chip maker can manufacture just one gate type and still build any circuit. That uniformity simplifies fabrication.

blocks.subTitle: What a multiplexer is for
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a multiplexer used for?**

It picks one of several input signals to pass through, based on a select input. CPUs use muxes constantly — for example, an ALU computes several possible results in parallel, then a mux selects the one the current instruction actually needs.

blocks.subTitle: Half adder vs full adder
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Half adder vs full adder — what's the real difference?**

A half adder adds two bits and has no carry-in, so it can only handle the lowest bit column. A full adder adds two bits plus a carry-in, so full adders can be chained to add numbers of any width, one column at a time.
